media.title: Marble head of an athlete
media.author: Roman, copy of a Greek work
media.license: CC0 (The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access)
media.note: Cut out from its backdrop and post; the albedo, normal/height and aux (wide normal, thickness, polish) maps were derived offline from this single photograph, with Depth Anything V2 Small (Apache-2.0) for the large form.

credits.readme:
- Photograph: *Marble head of an athlete*, Roman, Antonine, ca. 138–192 CE,
  The Metropolitan Museum of Art (248579), Open Access, CC0. Details in
  `assets/credits.json`.
- Depth: Depth Anything V2 Small (Yang et al., 2024; Apache-2.0), run
  offline; nothing of it ships.
- Shading after pre-integrated skin shading (Penner, 2011) and the
  wrap-lighting and thickness-map translucency of real-time SSS (Green, GPU
  Gems 1; Barré-Brisebois and Bouchard, 2011). No third-party code in the
  component.

files.text:
By torchlight

The Greeks went a long way for their marble. The best came from Paros, in the middle of the Cyclades, where the quarrymen followed the purest vein underground and cut it in galleries so deep that they worked by lamplight; the stone was called lychnites, lamp-stone, and Pliny thought that was why. Athens had its own mountain, Pentelikon, ten miles from the Acropolis, a fine, even white with a trace of iron in it that has turned the Parthenon the colour of honey in twenty-five centuries of weather. The Romans, when they had money enough, shipped Greek stone to Italy, until under Augustus they opened the quarries above Luna on the Tuscan coast, the mountain we call Carrara, which was still being cut for Michelangelo fifteen hundred years later and is still being cut today.

What they wanted from it was not only whiteness. Marble is limestone that has been buried, heated and squeezed until it has grown again into a mass of interlocking crystals of calcite, each one clear, and light that falls on it does not stop at the surface. It goes in, a few millimetres, rather more in a good Parian, glancing from one crystal face to the next, and comes out again a little way from where it entered, softened and faintly warm. That is why a marble cheek seems to have depth under it, and why the edge of an ear or a nostril, or the tip of a curl, glows when the light is behind it, while plaster, which turns every ray back at the surface, looks like chalk. It is very nearly what skin does, and sculptors have always known it.

They also helped it. Vitruvius, writing for Augustus, gives the recipe for ganosis: Punic wax melted with a little oil and laid on with a brush, then warmed with a pan of coals held close until it sweats into the surface, and rubbed with a candle and clean linen cloths, “as the naked marble statues are cared for.” Accounts from the sanctuary on Delos record payments for exactly this, along with the oil and the sponges and the cloth, to the men who looked after the statues of the gods. The wax filled the scratches left by the abrasives, softened the glare, and let the light go deeper still; under it the polished face and the rough, drilled hair answered the light differently, and the flesh looked like flesh.

By the eighteenth century the marbles of Rome stood in long galleries, lit from high windows, and the light of day was even and dull. So the custodians of the Vatican and the Capitoline would, for a fee, open the galleries at night and carry a torch among the statues, and it became one of the things a traveller did. Goethe went in the winter of 1787 and thought it the best way of all to see them: the torch, held close and moved slowly, picked out each part on its own and then the passage between them, the eye sockets filled with shadow and the cheekbone caught, and the stone that had stood all day like furniture began to breathe. Canova, it is said, showed his own new work to visitors the same way, at night, by the light of a single candle.

# marble-relight A marble head standing in the page, lit by a candle you carry. In a museum at night a guard's torch passes over a statue and it comes alive: the eye sockets fill with shadow, the cheekbone catches, and at the thin places (the rim of the ear, a curl standing free, the edge of the profile) the stone glows, because marble lets light in a few millimetres before it lets it out again. That glow is what makes marble read as marble and not plaster. Here one museum photograph of a Roman head becomes that statue: the pointer is the candle (on a phone, the tilt of the phone and a sideways drag), the head never moves, and its shadow falls across the paper and the words beside it. ```html ``` Or `import { marbleRelight } from './marble-relight.js'` and call `marbleRelight(figure, options)`; it returns `destroy()`. The `` is the plain cut-out photograph and sets the size. It is what shows without JS or WebGL, in print, and until the maps arrive. The maps are fetched only when the figure comes within 800 px of the viewport. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-albedo` | `albedo` | required | the photo with its studio light divided out; alpha = the cut-out. Its colour is carried out past the outline (saved with WebP `exact`), so it filters cleanly | | `data-normal` | `normal` | required | PNG, lossless: r g = surface normal, b = height | | `data-aux` | `aux` | required | PNG at half size: r g = a wide (blurred) normal, b = thickness, a = 0.5 + 0.5 x polish | | `data-height` | `height` | `400` | the range of the height channel, in texels of the normal map. Printed by the processing step | | `data-thick` | `thick` | `800` | the range of the thickness channel, in texels | | `data-light` | `light` | `-45 32` | where the candle rests: azimuth and elevation in degrees. Azimuth is on the screen: `0` = from the top, `-90` = from the left, so `-45` is the flattering three-quarter light from the upper left | | `data-cast` | `cast` | `0.7` | 0-1, how dark the shadow on the paper is | | `data-muted` | `muted` | `0.45` | 0-1, how far the stone's colour is muted toward grey (the candle adds its own warmth) | | `data-reach` | `reach` | `5` | in head radii: past this distance the pointer stops carrying the candle and it drifts back to rest | | `data-glow` | `glow` | `1` | scales how far light travels in the stone (the translucency). `0` gives plaster | The options object wins over the attributes. ## How the candle moves - **Desktop:** the pointer is the candle. Its direction from the head's centre is the side the light comes from; its distance sets how high it is held: over the face it is up in front (66°), a head's height away it is down at the side (10°), so below the head is the museum-at-night look and beside it is raking light. Past `reach` it drifts back to rest; leave the window and it goes back to rest. - **Phone:** turning the phone left and right carries the candle up to ±110° round the head; tipping it toward or away from you lowers or raises it (`tilt.js`, shared and smoothed, its level drifting back over about 12 s). A sideways drag on the head carries it too (260° across the screen); a vertical swipe scrolls the page as usual (`touch-action: pan-y`). Six and a half seconds after the last touch the drag is let go and the candle returns. - **Keyboard:** the figure is focusable. Left and right arrows carry the candle round by 20°, up and down raise and lower it by 6°; Escape sends it back. - **A hand-held candle.** It follows through a critically damped spring (`STIFF = 4.6`/s): a little lag, no overshoot. The first time the head is seen, the candle arrives from below and settles at the three-quarter light (about two seconds, once). - **Flicker.** While the candle is carried its flame gutters a little (±4-5% brightness, a fraction of a degree of wobble). Held still in still air a flame stands up and steadies, so about 1.4 s after the candle stops, the flicker has faded and the loop stops. This is deliberate: a flame that flickered forever would keep the GPU busy on an idle page. ## How it works **Offline (Python), from one evenly lit photograph** (the Met's left profile, 4000 px tall, the head about 2900 px): 1. **Cut-out:** the backdrop is a grey gradient, so it is modelled per row from the outer columns; a Lab distance (mostly chroma) seeds GrabCut; the steel post is walked out column by column from below until solid bright marble, and the neck's broken lower edge is drawn straight across where the post went in. Signed-distance alpha, about a pixel of anti-aliasing. 2. **Large form:** the silhouette is *inflated*: solve ∇²u = −1 inside the outline (conjugate gradients at half size) and take √u, which gives round, smooth cross-sections with no crease along the middle (a distance transform has one, and it shows as a ridge under a low light). That is modulated by the low frequencies of **Depth Anything V2 Small** (`depth-anything/Depth-Anything-V2-Small-hf`, run locally at 1904 px), and the model's middle frequencies are added on top: the snail-shell volume of each curl, the ear, the brow. A real head is about 0.36 of its width deep on the visible side, which sets the scale. 3. **Fine carving** from luminance (dark = deep under soft light), band-passed at four scales, **with stains taken out first**: on the smooth face and neck the only darkening is stain, so the luminance band-pass is regressed on the chroma band-pass there, and that much of each yellow-brown stain is removed before the carving is read. Shrinkage drops faint mottle, and a closing by line segments at eight angles fills any pit or speck shorter than 17 px whichever way it lies (weathering, dirt, sensor grain), while a drilled groove survives along its length. Kept shallow (5 px). 4. **Thickness** along the view: the solid is taken as mirrored about the outline, so 2 × the large form's height, except where something stands proud and narrow (a white top-hat at 12 px: the ear's rim, free curls), which is a thin flap whatever its height. 5. **Polish:** smooth, clean, bright = polished (the face, the neck); the drill-work of the curls and the weathered crown were not. 6. **Albedo:** the studio light is found by fitting ambient + one soft key against the wide normals over a grid of directions (it came out upper left, 40° up), divided out (to the 0.85 power), with a cavity term; the veining and the iron stains stay. **In the shader (only while the candle moves):** - **The candle is a point**, a little more than a head's height from the centre, so its light falls off across the head (1/d^1.8): the near side glows, the far side sinks. - **Diffuse, per channel:** red is lit through a normal 55% of the way to the wide normal, green 25%, blue the sharp one, with a wrap of 0.22 / 0.13 / 0.07. This is a cheap stand-in for blurring the irradiance under the surface (wider in red, as in pre-integrated skin shading): terminators are soft and warm, small carving stays crisp in blue. - **Light through the stone:** a warm fill wherever the candle reaches nearby (a shadow on marble glows a little, warm, under the stone that casts it), and light out through thin parts, `exp(−thickness / ℓ)` per channel (ℓ red ≈ 1.3 cm, green 0.8×, blue 0.58×) times how much the wide normal faces the candle. With `glow: 0` the same head reads as plaster. - **Self-shadows:** 40 geometric steps of a narrow cone toward the candle through the height field (the mip level grows a little with distance so thin features cannot alias into streaks; the first step is jittered by one whole step in log space so there are no bands). Penumbra widens with distance (a candle and its glow). Near the terminator the shadow hands over to the wrapped diffuse, so the march never cuts a hard line through a rounded cheek. - **Polish:** a faint Blinn-Phong highlight (60 and a broad 9) where the polish map says so. - **Room:** a dim, slightly cool ambient, darker in cavities (the height against a coarser mip), plus the candle's own light bouncing back off the room. - **Shadow on the paper:** its own canvas, larger than the head, drawn at 0.75 px per css px. The head's height (the normal map's blue, drawn small) is the body; each paper point marches 16 steps toward the candle in five side-by-side cones and measures how much of the candle's disc the head hides. Dark and sharp where it leaves the stone, softer and paler with distance, a narrow contact shadow all round the outline. It lies over the text. ## Tuning - In the processing: `HMAX` (depth of the head), `DEPTHW` and `MID` (how much the depth model shapes the form and the curls), `DETAIL`, the shrinkage and the `LINE` length, the flap top-hat size. Look at four light positions side by side before choosing. - In the shader: `wrapW` and the normal mixes (the softness of the terminator), `ell` and `uEll` (how far light goes into the stone), the fill weight (0.13), `uPen` (shadow softness), `uAmb`, the candle colour in `draw()`. - In the JS: `STIFF`, `DIST`, `EL_MIN`/`EL_MAX`. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | The candle and the room are not themed: the candle is warm, the room dim. The shadow on the paper is near-black ink at up to 50%; it is meant for paper. ## Behaviour and cost - **Nothing runs when the candle is still.** The loop runs while it moves and for about 1.4 s after (the flame steadying), then stops. Off screen, in a hidden tab or idle, nothing runs. Verified: 0 frames in 2 s idle. - DPR capped at 2 for the head; the shadow canvas is at 0.75. A head 540 css px wide is about 1.7 Mpx a frame with about 45 texture reads a pixel, plus the shadow pass: smooth on a laptop GPU while moving. - **Weight:** about 3.2 MB, all loaded only near the viewport: normal 1.8 MB (lossless; lossy compression shows as blocks under a low light), aux 0.64 MB, albedo 0.48 MB, the photo 0.34 MB. - Without WebGL, `createImageBitmap`, or if a map fails, the `` stays. If the GPU drops the context, the img shows until it comes back. ## Placement in the demo The head floats right in the essay, overhanging the column, and the text follows the profile: `shape-outside: polygon(...) content-box`, the outline traced offline from the cut-out's alpha at 41 heights. (An image `shape-outside` would be stretched over the margin box by the negative margins; the polygon on the content box is not, and it needs no JS, so the wrap is there in the no-JS page too.) Below 900 px the head stands alone between the title and the text. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The image is decorative (`alt=""`, `aria-hidden`); the canvases are `aria-hidden` and never take input. The figure is focusable with a default `aria-label` ("A marble head lit by a candle. Arrow keys carry the candle around it.") unless you set your own. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the candle rests at the three-quarter light from the upper left (the finished, beautiful state), with no arrival, no flicker and no easing. Hovering does nothing and the phone's tilt is ignored; a deliberate act still moves it, **instantly**: pressing on the head and dragging (mouse or finger), or the arrow keys. Chosen over "the pointer moves it instantly" because a light that jumps with every passing mouse movement is itself motion the visitor did not ask for. - Text under the cast shadow keeps its contrast (the shadow is at most 50% ink, usually far less where it reaches the words). - Print shows the plain photograph. ## Credits - Photograph: *Marble head of an athlete*, Roman, Antonine, ca. 138–192 CE, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (248579), Open Access, CC0. Details in `assets/credits.json`. - Depth: Depth Anything V2 Small (Yang et al., 2024; Apache-2.0), run offline; nothing of it ships. - Shading after pre-integrated skin shading (Penner, 2011) and the wrap-lighting and thickness-map translucency of real-time SSS (Green, GPU Gems 1; Barré-Brisebois and Bouchard, 2011). No third-party code in the component.
